alalal-c43449-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 2: whether God's being everywhere is the same as his being in every thing.

alalal-c43449-d1e113.summary: States the second question: whether being everywhere and being in every thing are the same for God.

alalal-c43449-d1e120.summary: First objection: the Philosopher calls the nature of place wonderful, so being in a place is more wonderful than being in a thing, and the two differ in God.

alalal-c43449-d1e137.summary: Second objection: not every thing is a place, so being in a place and being in a thing differ, also in God.

alalal-c43449-d1e150.summary: Third objection: God's being in things implies only a causal relation, but being in place adds the nature of containing, so they differ.

alalal-c43449-d1e166.summary: Fourth objection: if there were no place but heavenly spirits existed, God would be in every thing but not in every place, so the two are not the same.

alalal-c43449-d1e179.summary: Fifth objection: 'God is in things' converts with 'all things are in God', but 'God is in every place' does not convert to 'every place is in God', so the modes of understanding and what is connoted differ.

alalal-c43449-d1e203.summary: Sed contra: Lombard's text says that God's being everywhere is the same as his being in every located thing.

alalal-c43449-d1e219.summary: Second sed contra: the properties of place, containing, bounding and preserving, do not belong to place with respect to God, so God is said to be everywhere only as causing and conserving cause, which is also how he is in every thing; so the two are the same.

alalal-c43449-d1e249.summary: Albert's solution: they are not the same. Being in every thing denotes the relation of a cause conserving by essence; being everywhere or in every place further denotes that God holds place in being and gives it its power to contain the located, a power he does not give to every thing he is in.
claims: God's being everywhere adds to his being in every thing the giving of place's containing power.

alalal-c43449-d1e280.summary: Reply to the first two sed contra: Lombard does not mean they are identical but that one follows from the other: since place is a thing, if God is in every thing he is in every place; yet the preposition 'in' signifies a different relation in each case.
claims: Being in every place follows from being in every thing, but the relations differ.

alalal-c43449-d1e298.summary: Reply: God is in things as causing and conserving by presence of essence and power, but being in place adds a special effect, that he enables place to contain and preserve the located.

alalal-c43449-d1e316.summary: Reply to the second sed contra: the properties of place refer to God only as to their cause, but still being in place and being in a thing connote different things.

alalal-c43449.summary: Article 2 asks whether God's being everywhere is the same as his being in every thing. Objections stress that place is a distinctive nature, that not every thing is a place, that place adds containment, and that the two predications convert differently. The sed contra cites Lombard and argues that both are said only causally. Albert holds that they are not the same. Being in every thing signifies the presence of the conserving cause by essence and power. Being everywhere adds a special effect: God gives place its power to contain and preserve the located. Lombard means only that the one follows from the other, since place is a thing.
claims: God's being everywhere is not identical with his being in every thing, though it follows from it.
Being in place adds that God gives place its power to contain and preserve the located.
